text: Name something you'd find in a Great Ocean Road rock pool.

answers.note: Generic bucket. Named species (eleven-armed, biscuit, cushion, eight-armed) are separate rarer entries; host may merge them here if the table prefers.
Unqualified 'crab' and 'shore crab' land here (the shore crab is the most common crab on Victorian coasts). Hermit, decorator and spider crabs are their own entries.
Generic bucket. The red waratah anemone is a separate entry; host may merge.
Generic bucket. Kelp, bull kelp, Neptune's necklace, sea lettuce and coralline algae are separate entries.
Catch-all for unspecified shells and bivalves. Named shells (cowrie, turban, top shell, cone, abalone etc.) are separate entries.
Generic bucket. Blenny, goby, toadfish, pipefish, clingfish and seahorse are separate entries.
The little blue periwinkle carpets the high shore on every GOR platform. Note some Victorians call edible warreners 'periwinkles'; those land under Turban shell only if they say turban/warrener.
Cellana tramoserica (variegated limpet) is the big one on Victorian rocks.
Little black mussel beds (Xenostrobus) and blue mussels (Mytilus) both occur; 'muscles' is the inevitable misspelling.
Purple sea urchin (Heliocidaris erythrogramma) is the GOR rock pool urchin; empty tests and spines count too.
Generic bucket for unspecified snails. Periwinkle, turban, nerite, top shell, whelk, cowrie, cone and conniwink are separate entries.
Museums Victoria's rock-pool prawn (Palaemon serenus) is the near-transparent one kids chase with nets.
Unqualified 'octopus' lands here; blue-ringed is its own entry.

Genuinely lives in Victorian rock pools, including the Otway coast. Safety note for the table: never pick one up or poke under ledges bare-handed; the bite is painless and potentially fatal. Expect more guests to say this than you'd think.
Generic kelp bucket; bull kelp is a separate rarer entry because locals name it specifically.
Moon jellies and jelly blubbers do get trapped in pools at low tide. Bluebottle is its own entry.
Blacklip abalone sit in low pools and gutters on GOR platforms (Marengo Reefs is noted for them). Remind the table that taking them is heavily regulated.
The eight-plated 'coat of mail' mollusc under every low-shore rock; a school-excursion favourite in Victoria.
The dark-red anemone that closes into a blob at low tide on every Victorian platform; 'red anemone' or 'red blobs' maps here. Host may merge into the generic anemone bucket.
Turbo undulatus, the warrener: the green 'cat's eye' lids kids collect on GOR beaches are its operculum, so 'cat's eye' lands here.
Nudibranch and sea slug merged as one bucket. Sea hare and elephant snail are separate entries.
Technically correct and a few guests will say it; decide before play whether the lazy trio (rocks, sand, seawater) scores.
Technically correct; see Rocks note.
The smart-alec answer; technically correct. See Rocks note.
Generic bird answers land here. Oystercatcher and heron are separate (deep) entries. Host discretion on whether 'in' a rock pool is satisfied by a gull standing in one; lean accept.
Sad but true; accept. Thongs, fishing line, sea glass and driftwood have their own buckets.
Washes into pools after onshore winds; less frequent on the Otway coast than in NSW but a valid Victorian answer. Generic 'stinger' lands here.
Sea squirt and cunjevoi merged. The leathery brown mats at the low-tide edge that squirt when stepped on; more a NSW word, but Victorian platforms are covered in them. Sea tulip is separate.
Scutus antipodes: the big black slug-like mollusc with a hidden white shield shell, a classic Victorian low-pool find. A genuine local answer, not a joke.
Southern cowries (Notocypraea spp.) live under rocks on Victorian low shores; worn shells also wash in. Accept shell or live animal.
Dog whelk, mulberry whelk and cartrut shell merged here as the predatory snails that drill mussels and barnacles.
Under rocks in low pools; the wriggly skinny-armed ones. Separate from sea star by convention; host may merge.

aliases: big starfish with lots of arms
answers.note: Coscinasterias muricata, Victoria's biggest rock pool sea star; arm count actually varies from 7 to 14.
The Tasmanian blenny is the little dark darting fish in nearly every Victorian pool; 'blenny' is the right local answer rather than a generic fish.
Hormosira banksii, the string-of-beads brown alga every Victorian kid has popped; the single most characteristic GOR rock pool seaweed. 'Sea grapes' maps here in the southern-Australian sense.
The white calcareous tubes (Galeolaria) that crust the mid shore and shred your feet; fan/feather-duster worms merged here.
Live cuttlefish and washed-up cuttlebone merged; the bone is the likely find.
Joke-but-true; accept with a smile. Any people answer lands here.
Footwear bucket. Accept; genuinely a GOR rock pool regular.
Angling debris bucket; accept.
Not a dominant rock-platform species on the open Otway coast but present; accept.
Smooth toadfish does turn up in Victorian tide pools and gutters; accept. Remind the table they are poisonous to eat (and to dogs).
Accept; distinct from general rubbish because people hunt for it deliberately.
Very GOR after a blow; accept.
Durvillaea potatorum fringes every exposed GOR platform at low tide; the specific local name earns a separate bucket from generic kelp. Host may merge.
Generic 'worm' lands here (the free-living polychaetes under rocks). Tube worms and flatworms are separate entries.
Tosia australis, the stiff pentagonal star with biscuit-edge plates; Museums Victoria lists it in the lower intertidal. Genuine Victorian deep cut.
Parvulastra exigua, the thumbnail-sized green-brown pentagonal star in the thousands on Victorian platforms; the commonest sea star most people never notice.

Meridiastra (Patiriella) calcar, the carpet or eight-armed star: variably coloured, 7 to 9 arms, extremely common in Victorian pools. Listed by Marine and Coasts Victoria as a frequent rock pool find.
Small majid crabs that glue weed and sponge onto themselves; present in Victorian weedy pools. Accept 'crab covered in seaweed'.
Famous in Port Phillip Bay rather than GOR pools, but juveniles and moulted shells turn up in deep gutters. Host discretion; lean accept.
Ligia australiensis, the big grey isopod scuttling over splash-zone rocks; present at every GOR platform but rarely named.
Amphipods in the wrack at the pool edge; accept.

The pink crust and pink turf lining every Victorian rock pool. If a guest says plain 'coral', the host may redirect here (there is no reef coral in Victorian rock pools) or reject; decide before play.

aliases: the black bird with the orange beak
answers.note: Sooty oystercatchers work GOR platforms at low tide; a genuine local deep cut.
The grey heron-looking bird stalking fish in GOR pools is almost always the white-faced heron (locally 'blue crane'); eastern reef egret is rarer but merged here.

aliases: the slug that squirts purple ink
answers.note: The big brown slug that squirts purple ink when handled; listed on the Victorian rockpool ID sheet. Separate from the sea slug bucket because of the ink, which is how people describe it.
Stalked ascidians in the lowest pools and surge channels; accept.
Nerita atramentosa/melanotragus, the thick black snail with a white underside on the mid shore; Australian Museum and Victorian field guides both list it. 'Black snail' lands here.

Austrocochlea zebra and ribbed top shells are the black-and-white striped snails all over Victorian mid-shore pools; the Victorian rockpool ID sheet calls one 'striped snail'. Any striped-snail description lands here.
Bembicium nanum, the small conical ridged snail of the Victorian high-mid shore with the proper local name 'striped-mouth conniwink'. Pure deep cut; whoever says it wins the pool.
Siphonaria, the air-breathing 'false limpet' with a side notch, commoner on Victorian platforms than most true limpets. Deep cut.

aliases: flat wriggly thing under a rock

answers.note: Pycnogonids live among hydroids and weed in Victorian pools; accept.
The white lacy crust on kelp fronds and under ledges; accept 'lace coral'.
Spotted and wide-bodied pipefish hide in weedy Victorian pools; accept.
Clingfish and weedfish merged as the cryptic weed-dwelling pool fish of southern Australia; both are genuinely common in GOR pools.

Big-belly and short-head seahorses are Victorian natives but mostly subtidal; they do turn up in deep weedy pools and surge gutters. Host discretion; lean accept. Weedy seadragon is subtidal only and should be rejected.
Port Jackson shark corkscrew eggs and draughtboard shark/skate cases wash into GOR pools regularly. The egg case counts; a live shark does not.
Juvenile southern rock lobsters (crays) shelter in deep holes on GOR platforms and moults wash in; a Victorian would say 'cray'. Accept; it is not a trap.

Conus anemone, the southern cone, lives under rocks on Victorian low shores. Unlike tropical cones it is not considered dangerous, but it is a real local species, so accept; do not let a tropical-trap instinct reject it.

The shore platforms around Dinosaur Cove, Eric the Red and the Port Campbell limestone carry visible fossils, so a fossil in a GOR rock pool is a real answer. Host discretion; lean accept and don't let anyone chip one out.
Pedantic but correct; accept.
Sea hare 'spaghetti' egg strings, nudibranch ribbons and whelk capsules are all common Victorian rock pool finds. Shark egg cases are separate.

hostNotes: Accept any plant, animal, object or substance plausibly found in or at the edge of a temperate Victorian rock-platform pool; generic answers (crab, sea star, snail, seaweed, fish, octopus, anemone) are their own buckets and named species are separate rarer entries, but the host may merge a species into its generic bucket if the table prefers, and should decide before play whether the lazy trio (seawater, rocks, sand) scores. Blue-ringed octopus is a genuine Victorian rock pool resident and more guests will say it than you expect, so accept it and remind everyone never to pick one up; cone shell, cray/lobster and seahorse are real southern species too, so do not reject them on tropical instinct.
